## Overview of Pancreatic Tumors

- The pancreas gives rise to a diverse spectrum of neoplasms
- **Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)** is the most common (>90%)
- Other categories include:
  - Precursor lesions (PanIN)
  - Cystic neoplasms (IPMN, MCN, serous tumors)
  - Neuroendocrine neoplasms
  - Acinar cell tumors
  - Mesenchymal tumors
  - Ampullary/periampullary tumors
- Prognosis varies dramatically by type and stage

## Classification of Pancreatic Neoplasms

| Category | Examples |
|----------|----------|
| Ductal/ductal-related | PDAC, PanIN, IPMN, MCN |
| Neuroendocrine | PanNET, PanNEC |
| Acinar | Acinar cell carcinoma, Pancreatoblastoma |
| Cystic | Serous cystadenoma, Lymphoepithelial cyst |
| Mesenchymal | Sarcomas, GIST, Schwannoma |
| Uncertain lineage | Solid pseudopapillary neoplasm |
| Ampullary | Adenoma, Adenocarcinoma, NET |

## Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN) - Introduction

- Noninvasive lesion confined to pancreatic ducts
- Observed only microscopically (<0.5 cm)
- Mucin-containing duct epithelium with spectrum of atypia
- **Low-grade**: PanIN-1 and PanIN-2
- **High-grade dysplasia**: PanIN-3
- High-grade PanIN is the key precursor of PDAC
- Staged as **carcinoma in situ**

## PanIN - Epidemiology

- Low-grade PanIN associated with:
  - Age
  - Obesity
  - Diabetes mellitus (DM)
- Found in >50% of people older than 50 years
- High-grade PanIN is virtually indicative of invasive adenocarcinoma
- When PanIN-3 identified without established invasive carcinoma → thorough re-examination required

## PanIN - Pathologic Features (Low-Grade)

- **PanIN-1**: Flat or mildly papillated mucinous epithelium
  - Small, basally oriented nuclei
  - Mild to moderate nuclear atypia
- **PanIN-2**: Mildly enlarged basally oriented nuclei
  - Increased papillary architecture
  - Preserved cellular polarity

## PanIN - Pathologic Features (High-Grade)

- **PanIN-3** features:
  - Increased architectural complexity
  - Prominent epithelial papillation
  - Cribriforming
  - Budding micropapillae
  - Loss of cellular polarity
  - Marked cytologic atypia with nuclear pleomorphism
  - Frequent mitosis
- Biomarkers mirror ductal adenocarcinoma: **MUC1+**, abnormal **CEA** expression

## PanIN - Figure 59.1

**Figure 59.1: Pancreatic Intraepithelial Neoplasia (PanIN)**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | PanIN-1: Small basally oriented nuclei, flat to minimally papillated mucinous epithelium |
| B | PanIN-2: Mildly enlarged basally oriented nuclei, increased papillary architecture |

## PanIN - Molecular Biology and Genetics

- **KRAS mutations**: Present in most PanINs (both high- and low-grade)
- Significantly increased clonality in high-grade PanINs
- High-grade PanIN shares with invasive PDAC:
  - Biallelic inactivation of **CDKN2A (p16)**
  - Wide spectrum of clonal copy number changes
- High-grade PanIN **lacks**:
  - **TP53** mutations
  - **SMAD4** mutations
- These mutations are commonly seen in invasive ductal adenocarcinoma

## PanIN - Clinical Significance

- High-grade PanIN at resection margin = **microscopically positive margin (R1)**
- Presence of PanIN-3 → search for occult/overlooked early-stage adenocarcinoma
- Molecular progression model:
  - KRAS → CDKN2A → TP53 → SMAD4
  - Progressive accumulation correlates with histologic grade

## Ductal Adenocarcinoma - Definition & Variants

- **PDAC**: Aggressive malignant epithelial neoplasm derived from pancreatic duct
- Predominant glandular/tubular differentiation ± mucin production
- **Variants include:**
  - Adenosquamous carcinoma
  - Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC)
  - Colloid carcinoma
  - Anaplastic undifferentiated carcinoma
  - Sarcomatoid undifferentiated carcinoma
  - Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclastic giant cells
  - Medullary carcinoma
  - Hepatoid carcinoma
  - Signet ring cell carcinoma
  - Mixed ductal and nonductal carcinoma

## PDAC - Epidemiology

- Most common neoplasm of pancreas (>90%)
- Most cases sporadic; ~10% have familial history
- Deleterious germline mutation identified in 10-20% of familial cases
- **Location**: Head of pancreas (2/3) > distal portion
- Rare occurrence in pancreatic heterotopia (upper GI tract)
- **Median age at diagnosis**: ~70 years

## PDAC - Clinical Features

- **Most common presentations:**
  - Unexplained weight loss
  - Back pain
  - Jaundice
  - Decreased appetite
  - New-onset diabetes mellitus
- **Rare symptoms:**
  - Migratory thrombophlebitis
  - Acute pancreatitis (AP)

## PDAC - Diagnosis

- **Imaging:**
  - CT scans with multiphase-dynamic contrast
  - MRI
  - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) for sampling
- **Serum biomarkers:**
  - CEA (may be elevated)
  - CA 19-9 (may be elevated)
- EUS facilitates tissue sampling of mass/lymph node for definitive diagnosis

## PDAC - Prognosis and Treatment

- Overall 5-year survival: **<10%**
- Complete surgical resection + adjuvant therapy:
  - 5-year survival: 12-20%
  - Only ~20% of patients eligible at diagnosis
- Neoadjuvant therapy may improve resectability
- Untreated/metastatic PDAC: mean survival **<6 months**

## PDAC - Macroscopic Appearance

- Solid, firm mass with irregular contour
- Mean size of resectable lesions: ~3.5 cm
- Distal pancreas tumors usually larger
- Focal cystic changes distal to tumor (duct obstruction)
- **Head tumors**: Obstruct CBD and main pancreatic duct
- May infiltrate: ampulla, duodenal wall, SMV, uncinate process, retroperitoneum

## PDAC - Figure 59.2

**Figure 59.2: Macroscopic Appearance of PDAC**

- Ductal adenocarcinoma (*) in head of pancreas near uncinate process
- Obstructs pancreatic duct (PD)
- Impinges common bile duct (CBD)
- Causes **distal dilatation of both ducts**
- Classic "double duct sign" on imaging

## PDAC - Microscopic Features (Conventional)

- Most PDAC has **gland formation** with significant heterogeneity
- Distorted glands/tubules of varying sizes and shapes
- Large glands: cribriform and papillary pattern
- Small units: incomplete gland/tubular structure or single cell-infiltrating pattern
- Intracellular and extracellular mucin common
- **Desmoplastic reaction** surrounding malignant epithelium is typical
- Some cases: hypocellular stroma with dense pink collagen

## PDAC - Cytologic Features

- Epithelium: columnar or cuboidal
- Considerable nuclear pleomorphism
- Irregular nuclear membrane with smudged appearance
- Better differentiated PDAC:
  - Well-formed glands
  - Vesicular/foamy intracellular mucin
  - Condensed, thickened apical border of cytoplasmic membrane
- Metastases (lung, omentum): paradoxically better differentiation

## PDAC - Figure 59.3

**Figure 59.3: Microscopic Appearance of PDAC**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Primary PDAC with histologic and cytologic heterogeneity |
| B | Primary PDAC with foamy intracellular mucin and thickened atypical cytoplasmic membrane |
| C | Metastatic PDAC to lung showing paradoxical better differentiation |

## PDAC - Immunoprofile

- **Pancreatobiliary phenotype** (not entirely specific)
- Workup = diagnosis of exclusion from other primary sites
- **Positive**: CK7, MUC1, CEA, CA125, B72.3
- **Negative**: CK20, CDX2
- **DPC4/SMAD4 mutation** → loss of nuclear SMAD4
- **CDKN2A mutation** → loss of p16 expression

## PDAC - Molecular Biology

**Somatic genetic drivers:**

| Gene | Frequency |
|------|-----------|
| KRAS (oncogenic) | >90% |
| CDKN2A | ~80% |
| TP53 | ~75% |
| SMAD4 | ~55% |

- Less common: PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51 (DNA repair/epigenetics)

## PDAC - Hereditary Susceptibility Genes

- BRCA2
- ATM
- BRCA1
- PALB2
- CDKN2A
- STK11
- PRSS1
- SPINK1
- DNA mismatch repair genes
- Majority of familial aggregations have uncertain underlying genetic abnormalities

## Adenosquamous Carcinoma

- Homogenous squamous cell carcinoma of pancreas is uncommon
- Varying extents of squamous differentiation with conventional ductal adenocarcinoma
- **Classification requires ≥30% squamous component**
- **Diagnostic pitfall**: Exclusively squamous carcinoma in small biopsies/metastasis
  - Raises differential of primary SCC from other sites (especially lung)
  - Lung is a common metastatic site for PDAC

## Neuroendocrine Carcinoma (NEC) of Pancreas

- Rare: <1% of pancreatic neoplasms
- Includes **small-cell** and **large-cell** variants
- Clinically, pathologically, genetically **distinct from well-differentiated PanNET**
- More akin to PDAC in pathogenesis:
  - Associated with adenocarcinoma component
  - Frequent **TP53** and **RB1** mutations
  - Inactivation of RB1/P16 pathway
- Requires: NEC morphology + immunoreactivity for chromogranin/synaptophysin

## NEC - Subtypes and Features

- **Small-cell subtype:**
  - Nuclear hyperchromasia and molding
  - Minimal cytoplasm
  - Loss of Rb protein expression (most cases)
  - Ki67 >80%
- **Large-cell variant:**
  - Challenging diagnosis in small biopsies
  - Overlaps with high-grade PanNET, acinar cell carcinoma
  - Ki67 >20%
- Partial NE marker immunoreactivity without morphology = adenocarcinoma with NE differentiation

## Colloid Carcinoma

- Usually derived from **intestinal-type IPMN**
- **Defining feature**: ≥80% of neoplastic epithelium suspended in mucin
- Tumor cells:
  - Focal poorly differentiated signet ring cell morphology
  - Majority: strips, clusters, or glands (well to moderately differentiated)
- **Immunophenotype**: CK20+, CDX2+, MUC2+
- **Prognosis**: More favorable than conventional PDAC
  - 5-year survival >55%

## Undifferentiated Carcinoma

- Lacks recognizable cell line of differentiation
- Hypercellularity with confluent growth pattern
- May have partial/complete loss of cytokeratin immunoreactivity
- Usually positive for **vimentin**
- **Subtypes:**
  - Sarcomatoid carcinoma/carcinosarcoma: malignant spindle cells ± heterologous elements
  - Rhabdoid morphology: SWI/SNF pathway abnormalities (SMARCA2/SMARCA4 loss)
  - Osteoclastic giant cells: CD68+, CD163+ (histiocytic markers)

## Mixed Ductal and Nondutal Carcinoma

- Includes:
  - Ductal-NEC
  - Ductal-acinar cell carcinoma
  - Ductal-neuroendocrine-acinar carcinoma combination
- Each component must be ≥30% for classification
- Discussed in corresponding sections of acinar cell carcinoma and NEC

## Tumors Associated with Cystic Intraductal Neoplasm - Overview

- Prominent intraductal papillary growth pattern
- Grossly visible cystic lesions (>5 mm)
- May involve main pancreatic duct or accessory branch ducts
- **Subtypes based on epithelial phenotype:**
  - IPMN (Intraductal Papillary Mucinous Neoplasm)
  - IOPN (Intraductal Oncocytic Papillary Neoplasm)
  - ITPN (Intraductal Tubulopapillary Neoplasm)
- Spectrum: low-grade → high-grade → invasive carcinoma

## Intraductal Neoplasms - Epidemiology

- Wide age range; more common in 50s-60s
- Head of pancreas > distal portion
- Lesions can be multifocal
- **IPMN subtypes by location:**
  1. Main pancreatic duct (prominent dilation)
  2. Branch ducts (isolated cystic lesion, no apparent main duct communication)
  3. Mixed main-branch duct type
- Symptoms: pain, chronic pancreatitis, DM, jaundice (nonspecific)

## Intraductal Neoplasms - Biomarkers & Prognosis

- Without invasive carcinoma: CEA/CA19-9 may not be elevated in serum
- May be elevated only in **cyst fluid** from aspiration
- **Prognosis:**
  - IPMN without invasive carcinoma: favorable (branch-duct 5-yr survival >85%)
  - Main-duct: higher risk of high-grade dysplasia, carcinoma, recurrence
  - IPMN with invasive carcinoma: 5-yr survival 35-90% (stage/subtype dependent)
  - Colloid carcinoma association → significantly better than conventional PDAC

## IPMN - Macroscopic Features

- **Main-duct IPMN:**
  - May involve portion or entire duct including ampulla
  - Mucin extrusion visualized by endoscopy/ERCP
  - Dilated duct filled with mucin and soft papillary projections
- **Branch-duct IPMN:**
  - May lack visible connection to main duct
  - Multilocular cysts filled with mucin
- **Worrisome features**: Size >3 cm, mural nodules, intracystic masses → higher risk of high-grade dysplasia/invasive carcinoma

## IPMN - Figure 59.5

**Figure 59.5: Macroscopic Appearance of IPMN**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Total pancreatectomy with multifocal IPMN involving entire main duct |
| B | Distal pancreatectomy with mixed main-duct and branch-duct IPMN |

## IPMN - Histologic Subtypes

| Subtype | Location | Architecture | Immunophenotype |
|---------|----------|--------------|-----------------|
| Intestinal | Main duct | Villous papillary, tall columnar | CK20+, CDX2+, MUC2+; CK7-, MUC1- |
| Gastric | Branch ducts | Gastric foveolar, usually low-grade | CK7+, MUC5AC+; CK20-, CDX2-, MUC2-, MUC1- |
| Pancreatobiliary | Main duct | Complex anastomosing papillae | CK7+, MUC1+, MUC5AC+; CK20-, CDX2-, MUC2- |

## IPMN - Intestinal Type

- Commonly associated with **main-duct IPMN**
- Villous papillary architecture
- Tall columnar intestinal-type cells
- Elongated nuclei with apical intracellular mucin
- High-grade dysplasia commonly observed
- Associated with **colloid carcinoma** when invasive
- Immunoreactive: CK20, CDX2, MUC2
- Negative: CK7, MUC1

## IPMN - Gastric Type

- Often found in **branch ducts**
- Gastric foveolar phenotype
- Often low-grade dysplasia
- High-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma can occur
- Associated with conventional PDAC or pancreatobiliary-type when invasive
- Immunoreactive: CK7, MUC5AC
- Negative: CK20, CDX2, MUC2, MUC1

## IPMN - Pancreatobiliary Type

- Usually involves **main pancreatic duct**
- More complex architecture
- Anastomosing papillae of cuboidal cells
- Eosinophilic or amphophilic cytoplasm ± intracellular mucin
- Most have **high-grade dysplasia**
- Associated with conventional PDAC when invasive
- Immunoreactive: CK7, MUC1, MUC5AC
- Negative: CK20, CDX2, MUC2

## IPMN - Figure 59.6

**Figure 59.6: Histopathology of IPMN and Variants**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Intestinal-type IPMN in main PD with associated invasive colloid carcinoma (*) |
| B | Gastric-type IPMN with foveolar-type epithelium |
| C | IOPN with papillary growth and eosinophilic/oncocytic cytoplasm |
| D | ITPN with complex tubular/cribriform pattern, lack of intracellular mucin |

## IPMN - Molecular Biology

- **KRAS mutations**: 60-80% of cases (especially intestinal phenotype)
- **GNAS mutations**: 50-70% (unique to IPMN, not in PDAC)
- **RNF43 mutations**: ~50% of cases
- GNAS mutation distinguishes IPMN from PDAC
- Important for differential diagnosis and understanding pathogenesis

## Intraductal Oncocytic Papillary Neoplasm (IOPN)

- Variant of intraductal cystic papillary neoplasm
- Unique pathologic and molecular characteristics
- **Exophytic growth** with friable papillary projections into dilated ducts
- Back-to-back papillary or cribriform complexes
- Multilayered columnar cells with **eosinophilic (oncocytic) granular cytoplasm**
- Focal mucin-containing epithelium possible
- **IHC**: MUC1+, MUC6+, Heppar-1+; goblet cells MUC2+, MUC5AC+

## Intraductal Tubulopapillary Neoplasm (ITPN)

- **Least common** pancreatic intraductal neoplasm
- Predominant tubule-forming with PD epithelial phenotype
- **Lack of mucin production**
- Macroscopically: more solid, less cystic; intraductal growth hard to recognize
- Tightly packed tubules forming cribriform nests
- Cuboidal cells with scant eosinophilic/amphophilic cytoplasm
- Necrosis and high-grade dysplasia common
- **Invasive carcinoma in 70% of reported cases**
- IHC: CK7+, MUC1+, MUC6+; MUC2-, MUC5AC-

## IOPN & ITPN - Molecular Genetics

- **IOPN:**
  - No defining genomic alterations in most cases
  - Recurrent mutations: ERBB4, ARHGAP26, ASXL1, EPHA8
- **ITPN:**
  - No defining genomic alterations in most cases
  - Alterations in chromatin remodeling genes: MLL1-3, BAP1
  - PI3K pathway genes
- Rarity limits molecular characterization

## Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (MCN) - Overview

- Cystic lesions lined by mucin-producing neoplastic epithelium
- Can exhibit low-grade to high-grade dysplasia
- **Noninvasive** = mucinous cystadenoma
- **Invasive** = mucinous cystadenocarcinoma
- **Defining feature**: Subepithelial **ovarian-type stroma**

## MCN - Epidemiology

- Almost exclusively in **women (>98%)**
- Mean onset age: **48 years**
- Cystadenocarcinoma patients 5-10 years older than cystadenoma
- Suggests malignant progression from adenoma → carcinoma
- **Location**: Body/tail of pancreas (>98%)
- Radiographically: thick-walled cystic lesions **without communication** with pancreatic ducts
- Cyst fluid: elevated CEA (distinguishes from nonmucinous lesions)

## MCN - Prognosis

- **Noninvasive MCN**: 5-year survival = **100%**
- **Invasive mucinous cystadenocarcinoma**:
  - Depends on pathologic stage (tumor size, metastatic status)
  - 5-year survival: **26%**

## MCN - Macroscopic Features

- Median diameter: ~6 cm
- Fibrotic cyst wall ± peripheral calcifications ("egg-shell calcifications")
- Invasive carcinoma → larger tumors
- **Low-grade**: relatively smooth cyst lining
- **High-grade/carcinoma**: papillary projections, nodules
- Unilocular or multilocular
- Contains thick mucin or necrotic debris

## MCN - Microscopic Features

- Lined by tall columnar cells with abundant apical intracellular mucin
- Cyst wall may be denuded (lack epithelial lining)
- **Defining feature**: Subepithelial spindle cell-rich **ovarian-like stroma**
  - Nests of epithelioid cells resembling luteinized cells
  - Density varies with age (more cellular in younger) and size
- **Low-grade**: maintained polarity, minimal stratification, mild-moderate atypia
- **High-grade**: cribriform/branching, loss of polarity, significant atypia, frequent mitoses

## MCN - Invasive Carcinoma & Immunophenotype

- Invasive carcinoma recapitulates PDAC phenotype:
  - Conventional tubular adenocarcinoma
  - Adenosquamous carcinoma
  - Undifferentiated carcinoma with osteoclast-like giant cells
- **Immunophenotype:**
  - CK7+, CEA+ (pancreatobiliary type)
  - MUC1+ (cystadenocarcinoma)
  - May lose nuclear SMAD4
  - Ovarian-like stroma: **ER+, PR+**
  - Luteinized cells: α-inhibin+, calretinin+

## MCN - Figure 59.7

**Figure 59.7: Macroscopic and Microscopic Appearance of MCN**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Gross: unilocular cyst in tail of pancreas without PD involvement |
| B | Low-grade MCN: single layer tall columnar mucinous epithelium overlying dense ovarian-like stroma |
| C | Ovarian-like stroma immunoreactive to estrogen receptor |

## MCN - Molecular Biology

- Activating **KRAS mutations** (codon 12): 50-66% of cases
- **RNF43 gene alterations**: 50-66% of cases
- Similar to IPMN molecular profile
- Distinct from serous cystic tumors

## Serous Cystic Tumors - Overview

- Exact pathogenesis unknown
- Abnormal **VHL/HIF pathway** regulation in centroacinar origin cells postulated
- Vast majority are **benign** (= serous cystadenoma)
- **Subtypes:**
  - Microcystic serous adenoma (most common)
  - Oligocystic serous adenoma
  - Solid serous adenoma
  - VHL syndrome-associated
  - Mixed serous-neuroendocrine neoplasm
- Serous cystadenocarcinoma: extremely rare (1-3%), requires distant metastasis (<0.2%)

## Serous Cystadenoma - Epidemiology

- 1-2% of all pancreatic neoplasms
- 10-16% of operations for pancreatic cystic lesions
- Most discovered **incidentally**
- Age: 50-60 years (mean 58)
- **Female predominance**: 7:3
- >50% asymptomatic
- Nonspecific symptoms from local mass effect when present

## Serous Cystadenoma - Imaging & Prognosis

- **CT findings:**
  - Well-circumscribed, multinodular cystic/microcystic mass
  - Central scar with sunburst calcification (~30% of cases)
  - **No communication** with PD system
- **Prognosis:** Excellent (indolent behavior)
  - Surgical resection almost always curative
  - Radiographic observation appropriate for asymptomatic tumors

## Serous Cystadenoma - Pathologic Features (Gross)

- Most commonly in **body/tail** (>50%), solitary
- VHL-associated: multifocal throughout pancreas
- Size: variable (up to 25 cm)
- **Microcystic variant**: well-demarcated, numerous minute cysts (1-2 mm), sponge-like
- **Macrocystic (oligocystic)**: larger cysts (1-3 cm), unilocular/multilocular, no central scar
- **Solid type**: no cystic formation
- Do not communicate with PD system

## Serous Cystadenoma - Microscopic Features

- Cysts lined by **single layer of nonmucinous cuboidal epithelium**
- Sharp cell borders
- **Glycogen-containing clear cytoplasm**
- Homogeneously hyperchromatic, round nuclei
- **Capillary-rich network** underlying tumor epithelium
- Nuclear atypia and mitotic activity uncommon
- **Devoid of mucin** and mucin-related glycoproteins/oncoproteins (CEA, CA125, CA19.9, MUC1)
- Helps distinguish from mucinous neoplasms preoperatively

## Serous Cystadenoma - Figure 59.8

**Figure 59.8: Macroscopic and Microscopic Appearance of Serous Cystadenoma**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Gross: numerous minute cysts (sponge-like) |
| B | Microscopic: single layer cuboidal epithelium, clear cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei |
| C | VHL: co-existing serous cystadenoma (upper right) and neuroendocrine tumors (lower left) |

## Serous Cystadenoma - VHL Association & IHC

- **VHL disease**: 50-90% of cases
  - Multifocal (diffuse serous cystadenoma)
  - Microcystic or macrocystic form
  - No morphologic distinction from sporadic
- Also associated with:
  - Neuroendocrine neoplasms
  - Neuroendocrine microadenomatosis
- Mixed serous-neuroendocrine phenotype possible
- **IHC**: Low MW cytokeratins, broad-spectrum CK, EMA, MUC6, inhibin

## Serous Cystadenoma - Molecular Biology

- **VHL gene alterations** (familial and sporadic):
  - Somatic VHL mutations at 3p25.3: 50%
  - Loss of heterozygosity of 3p: 90%
- Allelic loss of chromosome 10p: 50%
- No specific morphologic criteria for malignant transformation
- Strict criteria for serous cystadenocarcinoma: **distant metastasis required**

## Lymphoepithelial Cyst (LEC)

- Benign unilocular/multilocular lesions
- Lined by **squamous epithelium** + surrounding cuff of **lymphocytes**
- Rare: <1% of all pancreatic cystic lesions
- **Male predominance** (M:F = 3-4:1)
- Mean age: 56 years
- ~50% incidental; others nonspecific symptoms
- Mean size: 4.7 cm
- Well circumscribed, no communication with PDs
- Filled with **chalky keratin debris**
- No dysplasia; reactive atypia possible

## Neuroendocrine Tumors - Historical Context

- Islet cell tumor first recognized by **Nicholls (1902)**
- Insulin discovered by **Banting and Best (1921)**
- Insulinoma reported (1924)
- Glucagonoma described by **Virginia K. Franzt** in first Whipple specimen (1940)
- Glucagon confirmed by radioimmunoassay (1966)
- Other functional tumors: gastrinoma (MEN-1), VIPoma (Verner-Morrison)
- Nonfunctional: initially "endocrine-inactive islet cell tumors"

## WHO Classification of PanNENs (2019)

| Category | Details |
|----------|---------|
| Pancreatic neuroendocrine microadenoma | <5 mm |
| Well-differentiated PanNET | Nonfunctional and functional (insulinoma, glucagonoma, gastrinoma, VIPoma) |
| Poorly differentiated PanNEC | Small cell and large cell |

- PanNEC considered a variant carcinoma (discussed with PDAC)

## Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Microadenoma

- Size <5 mm (arbitrary designation)
- Precursor of well-differentiated PanNET
- Especially in hereditary conditions and functional PanNETs
- **Distinguishing from enlarged islet/islet aggregate:**
  - Normal islet: normal glucagon (peripheral) and insulin (central) distribution
  - Microadenoma: clonal/abnormal hormone distribution or random expression
- IHC for glucagon and insulin delineates pattern

## Figure 59.10 - Microadenoma vs. Islet Hyperplasia

**Figure 59.10: Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Microadenoma versus Islet Cell Hyperplasia**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A-C | Nonneoplastic islet aggregate with normal central insulin and peripheral glucagon |
| D-F | Microadenoma: lacks insulin, clonal glucagon production |

- Key distinction: **normal vs. abnormal hormone distribution pattern**

## Nesidioblastosis - Clarification

- Term coined by **George F. Laidlaw (1938)**
- Greek: nesidion (islet) + blastos (builder)
- Originally: cells differentiating from PD epithelium to form new islets
- Previously synonymous with congenital hyperinsulinemia
- **1995**: Genetic basis identified = inactivating mutation in β-cell ATP-dependent K+ channel
- Hyperinsulinemia = **malfunction** (not proliferation) of β-cells
- Preferred terminology: **idiopathic hyperinsulinism of infant/adult**
- "Nesidioblastosis" NOT recommended for hyperinsulinism or islet aggregates

## PanNET - Classification Principles

- **Functional**: clinical evidence of hormone release + symptoms
- **Nonfunctional**: no clinical hormone syndrome
- Best classified by differentiation:
  - **Well-differentiated PanNET**
  - **Poorly differentiated PanNEC**
- PanNEC does NOT represent genetic progression from lower-grade PanNET
- High-grade PanNEN includes both G3 PanNET and PanNEC
- Mitotic activity and Ki67 are for **grading**, not classification alone

## PanNET - Pathologic Features (Gross)

- Sharply demarcated or encapsulated
- Small tumors: homogeneous, fleshy
- Partially cystic (degenerative changes) not uncommon
- Large PanNETs: bosselated/multinodular
- May show gross invasion into:
  - Peripancreatic tissues
  - Mesentery
  - Adjacent organs (stomach, duodenum, colon, spleen)
- Vascular invasion (especially splenic vein)
- Usually do not involve pancreatic duct
- Exception: serotonin-producing variant with duct fibrosis

## PanNET - Microscopic Features

- **Characteristic patterns:**
  - Loosely cohesive, nested
  - Trabecular/gyriform
  - Hyaline vascular architecture
  - Clear cell change
  - Pleomorphic type
- Delicate vessels separating tumor cell groups
- Hypercellular, stroma poor
- Copious granular eosinophilic/amphophilic cytoplasm
- Polygonal cells, no distinct borders
- Centrally/peripherally located nuclei (plasmacytoid)
- **Finely stippled ("salt and pepper") chromatin**

## PanNET - Grading & High-Grade Transformation

- Most PanNETs: **WHO G1 and G2** (low to intermediate grade)
- Can rarely progress to **G3**:
  - Mitotic activity >20/10 HPF
  - Ki67 >20%
- High-grade component usually not homogeneous
- Lower-grade counterpart often identifiable
- G3 PanNET rarely seen at initial presentation
- **Ki67 immunostain** helpful for detecting high-grade transformation

## Figure 59.11 & 59.12 - PanNET Pathology

**Figure 59.11:** Well-differentiated PanNET
- A: Well-circumscribed, fleshy lesion
- B: Trabecular pattern with low-grade cytologic features

**Figure 59.12:** PanNET with high-grade transformation
- A: Subtle morphologic alteration from low-grade (upper) to high-grade (lower)
- B: Ki67 immunostain better delineates grade transformation

## PanNET - Uncommon Variants & Differential

- **Oncocytic phenotype** and **clear cell change**:
  - Must distinguish from **renal cell carcinoma** (most common metastatic malignancy to pancreas)
- **Pleomorphic PanNET**:
  - Marked nuclear atypia
  - Can be confused with poorly differentiated/undifferentiated ductal adenocarcinoma
  - Despite bizarre cytology: usually NO increased proliferative activity
  - Does NOT correlate with unfavorable outcome

## Hereditary PanNET Syndromes

| Syndrome | Frequency of PanNET | Key Features |
|----------|-------------------|--------------|
| MEN-1/4 | 30-80% | Multiple PanNETs, microadenomas |
| VHL disease | 17% | Serous cystadenomas + PanNETs |
| NF1 | Extremely rare | Duodenal/ampullary somatostatinoma more common |
| TSC | Extremely rare | - |
| Mahvash disease | 100% by age 60 | Glucagon receptor mutation, multiple glucagonomas |

- All autosomal dominant except Mahvash (autosomal recessive)

## Hereditary PanNET - Pathologic Relevance

- Precursor microadenomas present in:
  - **MEN-1**: insulin- and glucagon-producing (pancreas), gastrin-producing (duodenum)
  - **Mahvash disease**: glucagon-producing
- Spectrum of abnormal islets → suspect hereditary condition
- Multiple PanNETs in MEN-1, VHL, Mahvash
- **Challenge**: symptomatic patient with multiple tumors → which is hormone source?
- VHL: serous cystadenomas can coexist with PanNETs

## Figure 59.13 - Hereditary PanNET

**Figure 59.13: Hereditary Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Hereditary PanNET with abnormal islets of varying sizes, microadenoma, and PanNET |
| B | VHL with serous cystadenoma (lower right) and co-existing well-differentiated NEN (upper left) |

## PanNET - Molecular Biology (Key Mutations)

| Gene/Pathway | Frequency | Role |
|-------------|-----------|------|
| MEN1 | 44% | Histone modification/remodeling |
| DAXX/ATRX | 43% | Telomere maintenance |
| MEN1/DAXX/ATRX combined | ~60% | Epigenetic regulation |
| PI3K/AKT/mTOR | 14.7% | Cell cycle, angiogenesis |
| KRAS, TP53, p16, SMAD4 | Usually NOT mutated | Distinguishes from PDAC |

- MDM2, MDM4, WIP1 amplifications (impaired p53 pathway without TP53 mutation)

## PanNET - Molecular Subtypes & Prognosis

- **MEN1/DAXX/ATRX-mutant**: worse prognosis, α-cell lineage gene signatures
- **MEN1/DAXX/ATRX wild-type**: heterogeneous gene expressions
- Epigenome plays critical role:
  - DNA methylation
  - Histone modification
  - Posttranscriptional regulation
  - Gene expression
- mTOR inhibitor (everolimus): improved survival in advanced PanNETs
- Germline mutations in CHEK2, MUTYH: 17% of sporadic cases

## Tumors with Acinar Differentiation - Overview

- **Acinar cell cystadenoma** (acinar cyst transformation)
- **Acinar cell carcinoma**
  - Acinar cell cystadenocarcinoma
  - Mixed acinar-NEC
  - Mixed acinar-neuroendocrine-ductal
  - Mixed acinar-ductal
- **Pancreatoblastoma**

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma

- Non-neoplastic cystic lesion lined by mixed acinar and ductal epithelium
- Proposed etiology: obstruction or metaplastic process
- <50 cases reported (under-recognized/misdiagnosed?)
- Any age; **female predominance** (3:1)
- Size: <1 cm to 20 cm
- All reported cases **clinically benign**
- No association with acinar cell carcinoma or pancreatoblastoma
- Multicentricity common
- Does not communicate with pancreatic ducts

## Acinar Cell Cystadenoma - Pathology

- Cysts of varying sizes separated by atrophic parenchyma or fibrotic septa
- Some filled with eosinophilic proteinaceous material
- Lined by 1-2 layers of simple cuboidal epithelium
- **Acinar differentiation**: granular intense eosinophilic cytoplasm apically, basal nuclei
- Intervening columnar ductal epithelium (±mucin) creates diagnostic challenge
- **IHC**: CK7+ (ductal), PAS+ diastase-resistant, trypsin+, chymotrypsin+ (acinar)
- Rare malignant transformation reported (acinar cell cystadenocarcinoma)

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma - Epidemiology

- Malignant epithelial neoplasm from acinar cells
- **Male predominance** (2:1)
- <2% of pancreatic neoplasms in adults
- **15% in children**
- Age: 60-70 years (range 2-88)
- Rare associations: FAP, Lynch syndrome, Carney's complex
- Large at presentation → mass effect symptoms
- **Lipase hypersecretion** → subcutaneous fat necrosis, polyarthralgia
- AFP may be elevated in young patients
- Median survival: 19 months; 5-year survival: ~25%

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma - Pathologic Features

- Average size: ~9 cm
- Fleshy, homogeneous, friable (hypercellular)
- Focal necrosis/cystic change (degeneration)
- **Hypercellular, minimal stroma, lacks desmoplasia**
- Sheets and large nests with lobulated growth
- **Acinar pattern**: resembles normal acini (minute lumina or solid eosinophilic rosettes)
- Other patterns: solid, glandular, trabecular
- Monotonous cells, mild-moderate atypia, prominent nucleoli
- Apical eosinophilic **zymogen granules** (highly suggestive)

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma - Diagnosis & IHC

- **Definitive diagnosis requires documentation of pancreatic enzyme production**
- Zymogen granules: PAS+ with diastase resistance
- **IHC:**
  - **Trypsin** and/or **chymotrypsin** (highest sensitivity)
  - **BCL10** (C-terminal; recognizes pancreatic lipase)
  - β-catenin nuclear reactivity: ~10% of cases
- Mixed acinar cell carcinoma: >30% of each differentiation line
- Mixed acinar-NEC: most common mixed type; shares genomic characteristics with pure acinar

## Acinar Cell Carcinoma - Molecular Genetics

- No consistent genetic alterations in most cases
- Small subset: SMAD4, CDKN2A, CDKN2B mutations
- APC/β-catenin pathway:
  - APC and CTNNB1 mutations: each <10%
  - APC gene loss: 48%
  - APC promoter hypermethylation: 56%
- **BRAF and RAF1 gene rearrangements**: 23% of cases

## Pancreatoblastoma

- Malignant acinar cell neoplasm with **distinct squamoid nests**
- Endocrine, ductal, mesenchymal differentiation possible
- More favorable in children than adults
- 5-year survival: 65% (resectable); 18% locoregional recurrence
- **25% of pancreatic neoplasms in early childhood**
- Median age: 4-5 years
- Associations: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, FAP
- Elevated **AFP** in 2/3 of cases (especially children)
- Rare: Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH)

## Pancreatoblastoma - Pathology & Molecular

- Large solitary mass (mean 10 cm)
- Hypercellular, lobulated, separated by fibrous septa
- Acinar differentiation: polarized eosinophilic granular cytoplasm or tiny lumina
- **Squamoid nests**: essential for diagnosis
  - Varying squamous differentiation ± keratinization
- Heterologous stromal elements (bone, cartilage) possible
- **β-catenin**: nuclear pattern in most cases
- **Molecular:**
  - Loss of chromosome 11p: >80%
  - CTNNB1 mutations (APC pathway): 50-80%

## Figure 59.14 - Acinar Tumors

**Figure 59.14: Histopathology of Tumors with Acinar Differentiation**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Acinar cystadenoma: mixed acinar and ductal epithelium |
| B | Acinar cell carcinoma: acinar architecture, polarized apical eosinophilic granular cytoplasm |

## Solid Pseudopapillary Neoplasm (SPN) - Overview

- Cell lineage **unknown**
- Striking female predominance (>85%) and young age
- Hormonal effect suggested but no endocrine imbalance documented
- Described in ovary and testis
- Suggested origin: genital ridges migrating to pancreas during embryogenesis
- 0.9-2.7% of exocrine pancreatic neoplasms
- ~5% of all cystic pancreatic neoplasms
- **Low-grade malignant neoplasm**

## SPN - Clinical Features

- Predominantly **young women** (mean age 28)
- No ethnic predilection
- Men: age of onset 5-10 years older
- Complete surgical resection curative in most cases
- Metastasis: <15% (liver or peritoneum)
- Even with metastasis: protracted course
  - **10-year disease-specific survival: 96%**
- Rare highly aggressive cases: transformation to high-grade malignancy/carcinoma

## SPN - Gross Pathology

- Well demarcated
- Size: 8-10 cm at presentation
- Small: solid appearance
- Large: **cystic degeneration + intratumor hemorrhage**
- Calcifications in septa or wall
- Figure 59.15A: Large SPN with degenerative changes

## SPN - Microscopic Features

- Heterogeneous: solid, cystic, pseudopapillary structures
- Periphery may interweave with adjacent parenchyma (poorly defined margin)
- Round to oval cells, eosinophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm
- **Diastase-resistant PAS+ hyaline globules**
- Solid component: uniform cells, loosely cohesive, intertwined capillaries
- **Pseudopapillary**: detachment of cells distant from vessels → cells clinging to hyalinized/myxoid fibrovascular cords
- Nuclei: grooved/indented, finely dispersed chromatin
- Mitotic activity: nil
- Hemorrhage areas: foamy macrophages, cholesterol crystals

## SPN - Immunophenotype & Molecular

- **Characteristic IHC:**
  - **β-catenin**: nuclear/cytoplasmic (hallmark)
  - Vimentin+, progesterone receptors+, CD10+
  - CD56+, synaptophysin+ (less specific NE markers)
  - **Chromogranin: NEGATIVE** (distinguishes from PanNET)
  - Pancreatic enzymes: negative (distinguishes from acinar)
  - CD99: dot-like paranuclear
  - Cytokeratin: patchy or negative (never diffusely positive)
- **Molecular**: Somatic activating mutations in **exon 3 of CTNNB1**
  - Prevents β-catenin phosphorylation → nuclear translocation

**Figure 59.15: Macroscopic and Microscopic Appearance of SPN**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Gross: large SPN with degenerative changes |
| B | Microscopic: prominent papillary structure |

## Mesenchymal Tumors - Overview

- Primary mesenchymal/nonepithelial neoplasms: **1-2% of pancreatic tumors**
- Classification similar to same neoplasms arising outside pancreas
- Can be solid or cystic
- Challenging to distinguish from epithelial neoplasms clinically/radiographically
- **Benign**: Teratoma, Lymphangioma, Schwannoma, Ganglioneuroma, Granular cell tumor, Desmoid, Leiomyoma, Lipoma, PEComa, Paraganglioma
- **Malignant**: Leiomyosarcoma, Liposarcoma, PNET/EES, E-GIST, SFT, IMT

## Mature Cystic Teratoma (Dermoid Cyst)

- Germ cell origin
- Pancreas: least common site
- Majority composed of **ectodermal elements** (hair follicles, sebaceous glands, skin)
- Mean age: 36 years (4 months to 74 years)
- Mean size: 7-8 cm (2-20 cm)
- Heterogeneous: solid and cystic areas
- Contents: pasty, hair, keratinous debris, sebaceous material
- Cyst wall: squamous, respiratory, or glandular epithelium
- All reported pancreatic cases: **mature (benign)**
- Excellent prognosis with complete resection

## Lymphangioma

- Benign tumor from lymphatic system
- Pancreatic: <1% of all abdominal lymphangiomas
- Possible etiology: congenital lymphatic malformation → obstruction → lymphangiectasia
- More common in women; all age groups
- **Macroscopic**: multilocular cystic, interconnected (dilated lymphatics)
- Contents: chylous, serous, or serosanguineous fluid
- **Microscopic**: cystic or cavernous subtype; endothelial-lined walls
- **IHC**: CD31+, D2-40+; CD34-; epithelial markers negative
- **Diagnosis**: Cyst fluid triglyceride >5000 mg/dL
- Surgical excision curative; incomplete resection → recurrence

## Schwannoma

- Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor (Schwann cells)
- Extremely rare in pancreas (37 reported cases)
- Adults; equal sex distribution
- Arises from autonomic sympathetic/parasympathetic nerves
- More common: head, body, uncinate; less: tail
- Average size: 9 cm (2-20 cm)
- Well-circumscribed, encapsulated
- **Histology**: Antoni-A (hypercellular) + Antoni-B (hypocellular) spindle cells
- Peripheral lymphocytes; myxoid changes in hypocellular areas
- **IHC: S100 diffusely positive**
- Multiple schwannomas → neurofibromatosis type 2

## Ganglioneuroma & Granular Cell Tumor

**Ganglioneuroma:**
- Benign; arises from sympathetic ganglion cells
- Exceedingly rare in pancreas
- Average size: ~8 cm
- Firm, well-circumscribed (not encapsulated)
- Schwann cells + mature ganglion cells
- IHC: NSE+, neurofilament+, synaptophysin+
- Complete resection; recurrence rare

**Granular Cell Tumor:**
- Benign nerve sheath origin
- May mimic ductal adenocarcinoma
- Eosinophilic granular cytoplasm, small inconspicuous nuclei
- **IHC: S100+**

## Desmoid Tumor

- Locally aggressive mesenchymal tumor
- Associated with **FAP and Gardner syndrome**
- 10 cases described in pancreas
- No metastatic potential; locally aggressive
- Homogeneous, firm, white; infiltrative borders
- Bland fibroblasts in collagen matrix
- Low-grade; no pleomorphism, atypia, or significant mitoses
- **Nuclear β-catenin+** (distinguishes from other spindle cell neoplasms)
- Recurrence: 20-75% (higher in FAP/Gardner)
- Differential: SFT, GIST, low-grade sarcoma

## Leiomyoma, Lipoma & PEComa

**Leiomyoma:**
- Exceedingly rare; from smooth muscle of blood vessels
- Spindle cells, cigar-shaped nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm
- SMA+, desmin+

**Lipoma:**
- Uncommon; mature adipose tissue
- Well-circumscribed, fatty
- Conservative management

**PEComa (Angiomyolipoma):**
- Very rare; strong female predominance
- Related to tuberous sclerosis gene complex
- Nests of epithelioid cells, clear/eosinophilic cytoplasm
- **SMA+ and HMB-45/Melan-A+; cytokeratin negative**

## Paraganglioma

- Arises from extra-adrenal paraganglia (neural crest cells)
- Retroperitoneal/peripancreatic location can manifest as pancreatic neoplasm
- Equal sex distribution; age 42-85
- Most nonfunctional (incidental or mass effect)
- Functional: catecholamine excess (palpitations, headache, hypertension)
- **Histology**: Zellballen pattern (nests with reticular vascular network)
- Abundant granular amphophilic cytoplasm
- Sustentacular cells surround nests
- **IHC**: Tumor cells chromogranin+, synaptophysin+; sustentacular S100+; **cytokeratin NEGATIVE**
- Key distinction from epithelial NET

## Malignant Mesenchymal Tumors - Overview

- Sarcomas represent **0.1% of all pancreatic malignancies**
- 10% of sarcomas arise in retroperitoneum
- Can infiltrate pancreas simulating primary neoplasm
- Classification/behavior similar to soft-tissue counterparts
- Types:
  - Leiomyosarcoma (most common primary pancreatic sarcoma)
  - Liposarcoma
  - PNET/Ewing sarcoma
  - Extra-GIST
  - Solitary fibrous tumor
  - Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor

## Leiomyosarcoma

- Most common primary sarcoma of pancreas
- Women > men; mean age mid-50s
- Can be very large (up to 30 cm)
- Cystic degeneration, hemorrhage, necrosis in large tumors
- **Microscopic**: Spindled cells in long, storiform fascicles
- Marked nuclear pleomorphism, eosinophilic cytoplasm
- **IHC**: SMA+, desmin+
- **Differential**: Undifferentiated/sarcomatous carcinoma
  - Carcinoma: partial muscle markers + some cytokeratin expression

## Liposarcoma & PNET/Ewing Sarcoma

**Liposarcoma:**
- Most common retroperitoneal sarcoma
- Up to 20 cm; wide spectrum of differentiation
- Well-differentiated: minimal atypia; needs ancillary studies
- **MDM2/CDK4 amplification** (FISH or IHC) confirms diagnosis

**PNET/Ewing Sarcoma (EES):**
- Rare; children/young adults; equal sex distribution
- Large solid masses (mean 8.2 cm)
- Small round blue cells, frequent mitoses
- **CD99 strong membranous+**
- **t(11;22) translocation** characteristic
- Cytokeratin may be positive (interpret with caution)

## Extra-GIST & Solitary Fibrous Tumor

**Extra-GIST:**
- <1% of all GISTs; exceedingly rare in pancreas
- Up to 13 cm; spindled or epithelioid
- **IHC: CD117+, DOG-1+, CD34+**; variable SMA
- Prognosis similar to small bowel GIST (relatively aggressive)

**Solitary Fibrous Tumor (SFT):**
- Rare; middle-aged to elderly women
- Short spindle cells around branching staghorn vasculature
- **IHC: CD34+, CD99+, STAT6+**
- Most indolent but not benign; rare metastases
- Doege-Potter syndrome (hypoglycemia) rarely

## Inflammatory Myofibroblastic Tumor (IMT)

- Low-grade; intermediate biologic potential
- Slightly more prevalent in women; wide age (0.5-70 years)
- Symptoms: abdominal pain, weight loss, palpable mass, obstructive jaundice
- Nodular, lobulated masses
- Spindled/stellate cells, myxoid to collagenous stroma
- Mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils)
- **SMA+**; ~1/3 cytokeratin+
- **ALK-1 immunoreactivity**: diagnostic hallmark (clonal ALK rearrangements)
- Favorable prognosis after resection; rare malignant transformation

## Lymphomas - Primary Pancreatic Lymphoma (PPL)

- Most pancreatic lymphoma = systemic disease
- **PPL**: localized to pancreas ± contiguous nodes/distant spread
- **Non-Hodgkin lymphoma** most common
  - DLBCL (most common subtype)
  - Follicular lymphoma
- 0.5% of pancreatic tumors; 0.6% of extranodal lymphomas
- Mean age: 63 (15-85); more common in immunocompromised
- Symptoms: abdominal pain, weight loss; **jaundice uncommon**
- Soft, white, fleshy mass; necrosis in high-grade
- **High complete response rate to chemotherapy**
- Accurate diagnosis crucial (different treatment from PDAC)

## Pseudotumors - Pseudocyst

- Circumscribed fluid collections rich in pancreatic enzymes
- Hemorrhage and necrosis
- Complication of pancreatitis; in children: after trauma
- **No epithelial lining** (inflamed fibrous capsule)
- Clinical history: repeated AP (alcohol, stones, trauma)
- Unilocular; varying sizes (up to 20 cm)
- Contents: hemorrhagic, oily, necrotic
- Microscopic: granulation tissue, inflammatory infiltrate, foamy histiocytes, fat necrosis
- **Cyst fluid**: markedly elevated **amylase**; low CEA
- Distinguish from mucinous neoplasms

## Pseudotumors - Retention Cyst

- Usually unilocular
- Dilatation of obstructed pancreatic duct (stones, inflammation, tumors)
- Isolated retention cysts: benign
- Can be distal to pancreatic adenocarcinoma
- Multiple with viscous content: cystic fibrosis
- Thin-walled; incidental microscopic to grossly detectable
- Smooth, shiny inner wall
- Lined by single layer cuboidal epithelium (mirrors normal PD)
- May show low-grade PanIN
- **Important**: examine proximal duct for occult adenocarcinoma

## Chronic Pancreatitis as Pseudotumor

- Benign chronic inflammatory/fibrosing conditions
- May be difficult to distinguish from carcinoma
- Alcohol abuse, duct obstruction, other inflammatory conditions
- Localized fibrosis → mass-forming lesions
- Certain subtypes especially form pseudotumors:
  - **Groove pancreatitis**
  - **Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP)**

## Groove Pancreatitis

- Localized chronic pancreatitis in **pancreaticoduodenal space**
- Between duodenal wall (1st/2nd portions) and pancreatic head
- Also: paraduodenal pancreatitis, cystic dystrophy of heterotopic pancreas
- Multifactorial: structural factors + stasis → PD obstruction → enzyme extravasation
- **Accessory duct of Santorini/minor papilla obstruction**: leading cause
- Typical patient: **males, 5th-6th decade**, alcohol/nicotine abuse
- Chronic relapsing course; can simulate PDAC

## Groove Pancreatitis - Pathology

- **Macroscopic:**
  - Thickened medial duodenal wall with mucosal nodularity
  - Fibrotic mass in pancreaticoduodenal space
  - Microcystic change
  - Foci of pancreatic parenchyma within mass
- **Microscopic:**
  - Dense fibrosis
  - Lymphoplasmacytic/histiocytic inflammation
  - Granulation tissue, microabscesses
  - Brunner's gland hyperplasia
  - Smooth muscle hyperplasia
  - Myoadenomatosis of duodenal wall
- Can cause duodenal stenosis, gastric outlet obstruction, biliary obstruction

## Autoimmune Pancreatitis (AIP)

- Also: lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis (LPSP)
- Up to 2% of all chronic pancreatitis
- Can be mistaken for PDAC radiographically/endoscopically
- **Type 1**: IgG4-related (high serum IgG4, IgG4+ plasma cells)
- **Type 2**: Idiopathic duct-centric (granulocytic epithelial lesions, no IgG4)
- Responds well to **corticosteroids**
- Associated conditions: multifocal fibrosclerosis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, Riedel thyroiditis, sclerosing cholangitis

## AIP - Pathologic Features

- **Gross**: Rigid pancreas, may lack discrete lesion
- **Microscopic hallmarks:**
  - Dense **periductal** lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates
  - Dense **perivenular** lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates (venulitis)
  - **Obliterative phlebitis**
  - Interlobular AND intralobular fibrosis
  - Acinar atrophy
- **Type 1**: Numerous IgG4+ plasma cells (diffuse, periductal)
- Figure 59.17: Rigid pancreas without discrete mass; no duct obstruction
- Figure 59.18: Periductal/perivenular infiltrates, fibrosis, IgG4 staining

## Heterotopic Spleen & Hamartoma

**Heterotopic Spleen (Splenule):**
- Within pancreatic parenchyma (distal pancreas)
- May mimic solid neoplasm radiographically
- Well-circumscribed, red-tan, <3 cm
- Unremarkable spleen tissue microscopically

**Hamartoma:**
- Benign tumor-like nodules of mature parenchymal elements
- Acini and/or ducts with distorted architecture
- **Lacking discrete islets of Langerhans**
- Sharply demarcated; average 3.3 cm
- Epithelial elements peripherally; fibrotic stroma centrally

## Metastatic Tumors to Pancreas

- Most common: lung carcinoma, GI carcinomas, lymphomas, renal cell carcinoma
- Secondary tumors: ~50% of pancreatic masses at autopsy
- Surgical resection specimens: lymphomas, RCC, melanomas
- **RCC and lymphomas**: prone to solitary pancreatic involvement without other metastatic foci
- Can mimic primary pancreatic carcinoma

## Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma

- Often solitary mass without other metastatic foci
- Amenable to surgical resection → long-term survival
- **Clear cell carcinoma**: most common subtype to metastasize
- Can manifest **>10 years** after initial kidney tumor
- Gross: well-circumscribed, fleshy, bright yellow-tan
- Microscopic: nests/sheets/cords, rich sinusoid vascular network, prominent clear cytoplasm
- **Differential**: PanNET (clear cell), solid serous adenoma, SPN clear cell, PEComa, ductal adenocarcinoma with clear cell

## Metastatic Melanoma

- Rare; primary sites: cutaneous and ocular
- Up to 13%: primary site not identified
- May mimic primary pancreatic malignancy
- Gross: black if intensely pigmented
- Microscopic: diffuse, noncohesive infiltration; wide morphologic spectrum
- Can mimic carcinoma, sarcoma, lymphoma (especially amelanotic)
- **IHC**: S100+, SOX10+, Melan-A+, HMB45+; **cytokeratin negative**
- Isolated pancreatic melanoma may benefit from complete surgical resection
- Unknown primary: equivalent or better outcomes than known primary

## Tumor of Ampulla and Periampulla - Overview

- Neoplasms at ampulla of Vater, minor papillae, periampullary duodenum
- **Epithelial types at ampulla:**
  - Intestinal-type duodenal mucosa (papilla surface)
  - Pancreatic duct epithelium
  - Biliary epithelium (distal CBD)
  - Common channel epithelium
- Neoplasms: intestinal, pancreatobiliary, or mixed phenotype
- Most are adenocarcinomas or precursor lesions
- Rare neuroendocrine tumors also occur here

## Ampullary Adenoma & IAPN

- **Two subtypes by location:**
  1. **Intestinal-type adenoma**: duodenal surface mucosa overlying ampulla
     - Similar to colorectal adenomas
     - Associated with FAP or Lynch syndrome
  2. **Intraampullary papillary-tubular neoplasm (IAPN)**: within intraampullary channel
     - Usually pancreatobiliary type
- Most asymptomatic when small
- Larger: jaundice, cholangitis, pancreatitis (CBD/PD obstruction)

## Ampullary Adenoma - Pathology

**Intestinal-type:**
- Tubular, villous, or tubulovillous configuration
- Nuclear pseudostratification of tall columnar cells
- High-grade dysplasia: cribriform glands, significant atypia, loss of polarity
- IHC: CK20+, MUC2+, CDX2+; CK7-, MUC1-

**IAPN:**
- Predominantly pancreatobiliary; ~50% mixed
- Exophytic polypoid masses in ampullary channel
- Complex villous/papillary architecture
- Cuboidal cells, round atypical nuclei, no pseudostratification
- >80% have both low- and high-grade dysplasia
- Treatment: endoscopic resection or transduodenal papillectomy

## Figure 59.19 - Ampullary Adenoma

**Figure 59.19: Ampullary Adenoma**

| Panel | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Adenoma (*) from duodenal surface mucosa at converge of distal CBD and PD |
| B | Intraampullary papillary-tubular neoplasm (*) within intraampullary channel |

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma - Epidemiology

- Ampulla: most common site for small intestinal adenocarcinoma
- 15% of all pancreatoduodenectomies
- Challenge: distinguishing true ampullary origin from secondary extension
- Median age: mid-60s
- **Presentation**: biliary obstruction → cholestasis, jaundice → relatively early diagnosis
- Periampullary duodenal subtype: GI bleeding (mucosal ulceration)
- **Better prognosis than PDAC:**
  - 5-year survival: 50% (localized), 28% (lymph node metastases)

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma - Origin & Gross

- **Origins:**
  1. Periampullary duodenal mucosa (± adenoma; prevalent in FAP)
  2. Intraampullary channel (± IAPN or flat dysplasia)
- **Macroscopic:**
  - Surface duodenal mucosa involvement: polypoid/ulcerated mass (endoscopically visible)
  - Intraampullary: relatively small, covered by intact mucosa, subtle raised nodule

## Ampullary Adenocarcinoma - Histologic Types

**Intestinal-type:**
- Associated with ampullary adenoma
- Resembles large intestinal adenocarcinoma
- Cribriform glands, tall columnar cells, elongated nuclei
- IHC: CDX2+, MUC2+

**Pancreatobiliary-type:**
- Shares morphology/immunophenotype with PDAC
- Simple/branching glands, cuboidal cells, round/pleomorphic nuclei
- Prominent stromal desmoplasia
- IHC: CK7+, MUC1+

**Mixed phenotype**: 30-40% of cases

## Ampullary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma & Other Variants

**NEC:**
- Rare phenotype of ampullary carcinoma
- Often arises with adenoma; may have mixed glandular/squamous
- Small-cell: fusiform cells, hyperchromatic, nuclear molding
- Large-cell: moderate cytoplasm, round nuclei, prominent nucleoli
- High-grade, aggressive; geographic necrosis common
- Requires chromogranin/synaptophysin expression

**Other variants:**
- Adenosquamous, mucinous, signet ring cell, medullary, undifferentiated
- Distinctive morphology but no specific clinical/genetic differences

## Ampullary Neuroendocrine Tumors - Overview

- Duodenal NETs: rare (2-3% of intestinal NETs), most diverse group
- Ampullary NETs: predominantly submucosa/muscularis involvement
- **Key entities:**
  - Somatostatin-producing D-cell NET (somatostatinoma)
  - Gangliocytic paraganglioma
- Together: ~30% of all duodenal NETs
- Associations: NF1, MEN1 (less in gangliocytic paraganglioma)
- Duodenal somatostatinoma: almost never functional (unlike pancreatic)
- Obstructive symptoms: AP, jaundice, intestinal bleeding

## Ampullary Somatostatinoma

- Glandular growth pattern with **psammomatous calcifications**
- Also: glandular carcinoid, psammomatous somatostatinoma
- Size: <1-3 cm; major/minor ampulla or periampullary region
- Calcification: 100% NF1-associated; 60% sporadic
- Infiltrates deeply into Sphincter of Oddi smooth muscle
- Abuts/invades pancreas without desmoplastic reaction
- Negative deep margins difficult with local excision
- Can be misinterpreted as adenocarcinoma in biopsies
- Bland cytology: round/ovoid nuclei, stippled chromatin
- Mitotic: 0-2/10 HPF (G1); Ki67 >2% → G2

## Gangliocytic Paraganglioma

- Polypoid/pedunculated ampullary/periampullary lesion
- Size: 1-3 cm
- **Unique trilineage differentiation:**
  1. Neuroendocrine epithelium
  2. Schwannian/nerve sheath component
  3. Ganglion component
- **IHC:**
  - Chromogranin+, synaptophysin+
  - Cytokeratin: negative in up to 50%
  - Pancreatic polypeptide, somatostatin, or VIP+
  - Schwannian component: S100+
- Lymph node metastasis: <30%; liver: <5%
- 10-year survival: >70%
- Most favorable outcomes after complete removal

## Figures 59.21 & 59.22 - Ampullary NETs

**Figure 59.21: Ampullary Somatostatinoma**
- Prominent glandular formation
- Bland cytologic features
- Psammoma body (upper left)

**Figure 59.22: Ampullary Gangliocytic Paraganglioma (GCP)**
- A: Endoscopic appearance of polypoid mass
- B: Trilineage differentiation: neuroendocrine epithelium (upper left), spindled schwannian/nerve sheath, and ganglion components (lower right)

## Summary - Key Diagnostic Distinctions

| Entity | Key Distinguishing Feature |
|--------|--------------------------|
| PanIN | Microscopic (<0.5 cm), ductal |
| IPMN | Intraductal, mucin, visible cyst |
| MCN | Ovarian-type stroma, women, body/tail |
| Serous cystadenoma | Glycogen-rich clear cells, no mucin |
| SPN | β-catenin nuclear+, young women |
| PanNET | Chromogranin+, salt-and-pepper chromatin |
| Acinar cell carcinoma | Trypsin/chymotrypsin+, zymogen granules |
| Pancreatoblastoma | Squamoid nests, children |
| Paraganglioma | Zellballen, cytokeratin negative |

## Summary - Molecular Markers in Pancreatic Neoplasms

| Tumor | Key Molecular Alterations |
|-------|--------------------------|
| PDAC | KRAS (>90%), TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A |
| PanIN | KRAS → CDKN2A → TP53 → SMAD4 (progressive) |
| IPMN | KRAS, GNAS (unique), RNF43 |
| MCN | KRAS, RNF43 |
| Serous | VHL (3p25.3) |
| SPN | CTNNB1 exon 3 |
| PanNET | MEN1, DAXX/ATRX, mTOR pathway |
| Acinar | BRAF/RAF1 rearrangements |
| Pancreatoblastoma | 11p loss, CTNNB1 |

## Summary - Prognosis Comparison

| Neoplasm | 5-Year Survival |
|----------|----------------|
| PDAC (overall) | <10% |
| PDAC (resected + adjuvant) | 12-20% |
| Colloid carcinoma | >55% |
| IPMN without invasion (branch) | >85% |
| IPMN with invasion | 35-90% |
| MCN (noninvasive) | 100% |
| MCN (invasive) | 26% |
| Serous cystadenoma | Excellent (benign) |
| SPN (10-yr) | 96% |
| Ampullary carcinoma (localized) | 50% |
| Acinar cell carcinoma | ~25% |
| Pancreatoblastoma (resectable) | 65% |

## Summary - Immunohistochemistry Quick Reference

| Marker | Positive In | Negative In |
|--------|------------|-------------|
| CK7 | PDAC, MCN, ITPN, Pancreatobiliary IPMN | Intestinal IPMN, colorectal |
| CK20 | Intestinal IPMN, colloid | PDAC, PanNET |
| CDX2/MUC2 | Intestinal type | Pancreatobiliary |
| Chromogranin | PanNET, Paraganglioma | SPN, Paraganglioma (CK) |
| Synaptophysin | PanNET, SPN (partial) | - |
| Trypsin/BCL10 | Acinar tumors | SPN, PanNET |
| β-catenin (nuclear) | SPN, Pancreatoblastoma, Desmoid | Most others |
| SMAD4 loss | PDAC (55%) | PanNET |
| S100 | Schwannoma, Granular cell, Melanoma | Carcinomas |

## Conclusion

- Pancreatic neoplasms represent a diverse spectrum of entities
- Accurate classification requires integration of:
  - Morphology
  - Immunohistochemistry
  - Molecular genetics
  - Clinical context
- Prognosis varies enormously (from benign to <10% 5-year survival)
- Hereditary syndromes play important roles in subset of cases
- Distinction between entities critical for appropriate management
- Multidisciplinary approach essential for optimal patient care

## *Key Takeaways:*

- PDAC remains the most common and lethal pancreatic malignancy
- Cystic neoplasms (IPMN, MCN, serous) have distinct management pathways
- Neuroendocrine neoplasms require careful grading and classification
- Molecular profiling increasingly guides diagnosis and therapy
- Ampullary tumors have better prognosis than pancreatic head carcinomas
